analysis.one_liner: Cuts Medicare Advantage insurer payments and automatically enrolls seniors in MA plans.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsor bill to overhaul Medicare Advantage payments has sat without a hearing or vote in two House committees since May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Starting in 2028, the bill would require Medicare Advantage plans to pay doctors and other providers a fixed per-person amount instead of fee-for-service, trim the benchmarks insurers are paid, stop bonus payments tied to quality ratings, and count only diagnoses from actual patient visits for risk adjustment. It would also automatically enroll every Medicare beneficiary into the lowest-premium Advantage plan available, make them stay in that plan or in Advantage for three years, fold hospice care into Advantage plans, and loosen ethics rules on equipment and drug referrals inside Advantage plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, if the payment trims reduce what the government overpays insurers. Beneficiaries would get hospice care included in Advantage plans, but they would lose the default option of traditional Medicare and the ability to switch plans freely for three years.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to pay providers on a capitated basis — a fixed amount per enrolled person — rather than fee-for-service, starting in 2028 [S2].
Cuts the payment benchmark for new plans to 75 percent of the blended benchmark beginning in 2028, and eliminates the quality-rating bonus increases plans currently receive [S2].

Limits risk adjustment to diagnoses documented on claims from face-to-face or telehealth visits, excluding diagnoses gathered through chart reviews and stand-alone health risk assessments — a mechanism that has been used to record additional illnesses and raise payments [S2].
Automatically enrolls every Medicare beneficiary into the lowest-premium Advantage plan available, with an option to opt out [S2].
Requires Advantage plans to include hospice care rather than having it carved out to traditional Medicare [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, whose payment benchmarks, bonuses, and risk-adjustment revenue would all be cut. Beneficiaries also bear a cost in choice: they could not switch plans or return to traditional Medicare for three years after enrolling in Advantage, except for a hardship like serious illness.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare Advantage insurers; enrollees' plan choice

drawbacks.text: After enrolling in an Advantage plan, a beneficiary could not switch to another plan or return to traditional Medicare for three years, except for hardship events such as serious illness as defined by the Secretary [S2].
The bill automatically places every Medicare beneficiary into the lowest-premium Advantage plan, making private plans the default rather than traditional Medicare, with only an opt-out [S2].

It creates an exception to the physician self-referral (Stark) rules for durable medical equipment and Part D drugs furnished under Advantage plans, allowing financial arrangements between referring doctors and suppliers that are otherwise restricted [S2].

Requiring capitated payment could make it harder for beneficiaries to keep seeing providers who are not part of a capitated arrangement, since plans could only pay providers that way, with only grandfathered plans and special-needs plans exempt [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The payment-cut side of the bill attacks real cost drivers in Medicare Advantage — upcoded risk scores, quality bonuses, and high benchmarks — and could save taxpayers money. But it buys that with a three-year lock-in that strips beneficiaries of the exit option that currently disciplines private plans, and it makes Advantage the automatic default for every new Medicare beneficiary. The loosened self-referral rules for equipment and drugs point in the opposite direction from the rest of the bill. As written, beneficiaries give up flexibility and choice in exchange for a leaner, mandatory private-plan system whose savings are not guaranteed to reach them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees in May 2025 and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since — only the sponsor's remarks on the floor in June 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. David Schweikert introduced the bill on May 15, 2025; no cosponsors joined [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, additionally, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce [S4].
The only recorded activity after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 3, 2025 [S4].
As of the latest record, neither committee has taken up the bill, so no provisions have advanced toward the floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, Medicare Advantage insurers, since none of the payment cuts, bonus eliminations, or auto-enrollment provisions have moved an inch — the current payment system remains untouched.

for.name: Rep. David Schweikert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the floor; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral in May 2025 — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.role: Industry with a stake in Advantage payment rules
against.what_they_did: No record ties the industry to this bill, but Advantage insurers have a long, well-documented history of mobilizing against Medicare Advantage payment reductions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition has formed in the record.

industries.note: The bill cuts insurer revenue on three fronts — lower benchmarks, no quality bonuses, and restricted risk-adjustment coding — while simultaneously making Advantage plans the automatic default for every new Medicare beneficiary and locking enrollees in for three years. Lower payments and a captive customer base genuinely pull in opposite directions.

industries.industry: Durable medical equipment suppliers and Part D drug suppliers with physician ownership
industries.note: A new Stark-law exception would let referring physicians keep financial relationships with entities furnishing equipment and Part D drugs under Advantage plans, arrangements otherwise barred as self-referral.
Hospice care would be folded into Advantage plans instead of remaining outside them, changing how hospice providers are paid and putting plans between hospices and Medicare.

analysis.trajectory: A one-sponsor bill with no cosponsors, pending in two committees with no recorded action after referral, rarely advances in a two-year Congress. Unless Schweikert recruits cosponsors or the provisions get attached to a larger Medicare package, this bill is likely to die quietly in committee at the end of the 119th Congress.
